scenario: AITA for not directly paying my friend for half of the gas used on a trip? | I will keep this short. We went on a trip and used two tanks of gas. 1 tank there and 1 tank back. I used my company gas card to fill up when we left our home city (the tank was on empty). When he went to fill up the tank on the way home he asked for half the money but I said no since I provided us with an entire tank to get to the destination. His argument was that since I didn't pay for it myself it didn't count, I think it does count since I still supplied us with half the tank and my method of acquiring the gas shouldn't matter. We did use his car but it shouldn't matter since we had used my car for the last trip which was roughly the same distance and it was his turn to provide the vehicle. AITA?

prediction.raw: This is a nuanced situation, and whether it was "right" or "wrong" depends on perspective, context, and how you and your friend view fairness. Here’s a breakdown of the key arguments and why your stance might be justified or not: ### **Your Perspective (0 = "Not AITA"):** You argue that: 1. **You supplied half the gas** (one tank out of two), so you contributed equally to the fuel cost. 2. **The method of payment (company gas card) shouldn’t matter**—the gas was still provided by you. 3. **Past trips followed a similar split** (you used his car last time, now it’s his turn to use yours), implying a balanced system. **Why this might be right:** - If you and your friend have a history of splitting costs fairly (e.g., alternating cars, splitting gas equally), your logic aligns with that precedent. - The company gas card was just a means of payment—you still covered the cost, even if indirectly. - His argument that "you didn’t pay for it yourself" is a bit of a red herring if the intent was to split the gas equally. --- ### **His Perspective (1 = "AITA"):** He argues that: 1. **You didn’t personally pay for the gas** (since it was a company card), so it doesn’t count as "your" contribution. 2. **The gas was used in his car**, so he feels entitled to half since he’s the one driving it. **Why this might be right:** - If he sees the company gas card as "free money" (not your personal funds), he may feel you didn’t truly "pay" for it. - Some people have a strict view that if you didn’t hand over cash, it doesn’t count as a contribution. - If you’ve never used a company card for personal trips before, he might not expect you to do so now. --- ### **Neutral/Compromise Perspective:** A fair middle ground could be: - **Acknowledge the company card was a one-time thing** (since you didn’t pay out of pocket) and offer to cover *half* of the cost from your own funds as a gesture of goodwill. - **Clarify expectations for future trips**—if you plan to use company cards again, agree upfront how that will be handled (e.g., "I’ll cover half the cost, even if it’s a company card"). - **Revisit past trips**—if you’ve never split gas before but used his car last time, maybe the gas split should be adjusted to account for that imbalance. --- ### **Final Verdict (0 = Not AITA):** **You’re not *technically* wrong**—you did contribute to the gas (even if indirectly), and if you’ve split costs fairly before, your stance holds. However, **his perspective isn’t entirely unreasonable** if he sees the company card as a loophole. **Best move:** If you value the friendship, consider compromising (e.g., paying half from your own money) to avoid resentment. If you’re firm on fairness, then your initial stance is justified—but be prepared for potential friction. Would you like help drafting a response to him?
